`LocalePrefixPattern.match` succeeds when the path begins with exactly that (`django/urls/resolvers.py:LocalePrefixPattern.language_prefix`, `django/urls/resolvers.py:LocalePrefixPattern.match`).

The matcher writes itself as the same prefix, so the route on the figure's match begins with `"nl/"` (`django/urls/resolvers.py:LocalePrefixPattern.__str__`).

`prefix_default_language=False` lets translations be added to a site that already exists without changing its addresses: the default language keeps the ones it had (`docs/topics/i18n/translation.txt`).

`LocaleMiddleware` chooses the request's language and activates it in its `process_request`, which runs before the handler resolves the path in `BaseHandler.resolve_request` ([Choosing a language: `LocaleMiddleware`](../i18n/choosing.md)) (`django/middleware/locale.py:LocaleMiddleware.process_request`).

`is_language_prefix_patterns_used` goes through the entries of the root resolver's list, and no deeper, and returns two answers: whether one of them has a `LocalePrefixPattern` for its matcher, and whether that matcher gives the default language a prefix (`django/conf/urls/i18n.py:is_language_prefix_patterns_used`).
The function looks nowhere but in that one list, and `include` refuses, with `ImproperlyConfigured`, a URLconf one of whose entries has a `LocalePrefixPattern` (`django/urls/conf.py:include`).

`LocaleMiddleware.process_response`, handed the 404, puts the active language's prefix in front of the path, asks the resolver through `is_valid_path` whether that resolves, as `CommonMiddleware` does for a missing slash, and if it does redirects to it (`django/middleware/locale.py:LocaleMiddleware.process_response`).

Given to `path` without parameters, it is compared with what is left of the path as text, so the hours' route matches `"openingstijden/"` while Dutch is active and `"opening-hours/"` while English is (`django/urls/resolvers.py:RoutePattern.match`).
Its regular expression, which reversing reads for every entry, is kept for each language (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._populate`).

The descriptor behind `regex` ([When a matcher's expression is compiled](patterns.md#when-a-matchers-expression-is-compiled)) expands the route's text under the active language, compiles it, and keeps the result in the matcher's `_regex_dict` under the language's code, so a read under a language not yet in it does all of that again (`django/urls/resolvers.py:LocaleRegexRouteDescriptor`).
`RegexPattern` has a descriptor of the same design (`django/urls/resolvers.py:LocaleRegexDescriptor`).

A `RoutePattern` takes its converters once, as it is made, from the route's text in the language active as the URLconf is imported, and `RoutePattern.match` looks up by name the converter of each group that the active language's expression captured (`django/urls/resolvers.py:RoutePattern.__init__`, `django/urls/resolvers.py:RoutePattern.match`).

`URLResolver._populate` files what it builds under the language that is active as it runs, and each of the three properties that read them calls it again when the active language has no entry yet (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._populate`, `django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver.reverse_dict`).

The scheme, host, query string and fragment of the URL it was given are put back around the new path (`django/urls/base.py:translate_url`).

It resolves the path before it activates the language it was asked for, so a Dutch address handed in while English is active does not resolve, and comes back untranslated (`django/urls/base.py:translate_url`).

Its one caller in Django is the view `set_language`, which redirects a visitor who has chosen a language to the page's address in that language ([The language views: `set_language` and `JavaScriptCatalog`](../i18n/views.md)) (`django/views/i18n.py:set_language`).
